segments.translit: paramamahānandasundaro hi kṛṣṇācārya[ḥ] punar api tam evārthaṃ pratipādayann āha—
segments.translation: [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}, beautiful with supreme great [joy]{ananda}, setting forth that same meaning once again, says:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), beautiful with supreme great joy, once again setting forth "that same meaning" (cp.11.m1). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has "great bliss" for great joy, and says instead that he spoke "to make the ultimate fully understood".

flags.note: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads slar yang de kho na bzhin du don dam pa rab tu rtogs par bya ba'i phyir gsungs te, "again, in just the same way, he spoke in order to make the ultimate fully understood": it has don dam pa, "the ultimate" (paramārtha), where the Sanskrit has tam evārthaṃ, "that same meaning", as if its manuscript read something like tathaiva paramārthaṃ. I translate the Sanskrit.

the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has mchog gi bde ba chen pos brjid pa, "splendid with supreme great bliss", for paramamahānandasundaraḥ; bde ba chen po usually renders mahāsukha ("great bliss") rather than mahānanda ("great joy").
The visarga of kṛṣṇācārya[ḥ] is Shastri's restoration; the sense is not affected.

segments.translit: nāṛītyādi| nāḍikā dvātriṃśanāḍikāḥ śaktis tāsāṃ madhye pradhānāvadhūtikā viramānandarūpā guruprasā[dā]t maṇimūle vidhṛtya khaṭṭāṅgam iti khaṃ śūnyatā (śūratā) prabhāsvare(ro)ṇa sahajaṃ saṃspṛśya| anāhataṃ ḍamaruśabdaṃ vīranādena śūnyatāsiṃhanādena naditaḥ san kṛṣṇācāryo hi kāpālikaḥ| dehanagarikāṃ praviśya pracāreṇa kleśabhakṣaṇadinayena ekākāratayā viharati bhramatīti|
segments.translation: "[Channel]{nadi}" and so on. The channels are the thirty-two channels, and the [śakti]{sakti} is the chief among them, the [avadhūtikā]{avadhuti}, whose form is the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}. Having held it firm at the [root of the jewel]{manimula} by the [guru]{guru}'s grace; "[khaṭvāṅga]{khatvanga}": kha is [emptiness]{sunyata}; having touched the [innate]{sahaja} with the [clear light]{prabhasvara}; having sounded the [unstruck]{anahata} sound of the [ḍamaru]{damaru} with the [hero's sound]{viranada}, the [lion's roar]{simhanada} of emptiness: [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} is the [kāpālika]{kapalika}. Having entered the [town]{town} of the [body]{body}, by [conduct]{carya}, that is, by the method of devouring the [afflictions]{klesa} and so on, he "wanders" in [one form]{ekakara}: he roams about.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the channel-śakti as the chief of the thirty-two channels, the avadhūtikā, held firm at the root of the jewel by the guru's grace; kha in khaṭvāṅga as emptiness; and the hero's sound as the lion's roar of emptiness. Entering the town of the body, Kāṇha roams in one form by devouring the afflictions (cp.11.m2).

equations.en: the chief of the channels, the avadhūtikā, whose form is the joy of cessation
the method of devouring the afflictions and so on

flags.note: khaṃ śūnyatā (śūratā): Shastri records śūratā, "heroism", beside śūnyatā. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has kha ni stong pa nyid, "kha is emptiness", which supports śūnyatā; I translate śūnyatā.
prabhāsvare(ro)ṇa: Shastri prints a parenthetical "ro"; I read prabhāsvareṇa, "with the clear light", as the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) does ('od gsal bas).

kleśabhakṣaṇadinayena: I read kleśabhakṣaṇādinayena, "by the method of devouring the afflictions and so on". the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has nyon mongs pa mngon par za ba'i tshul gyis, "by way of devouring the afflictions", with no "and so on", so the "di" may be a slip for kleśabhakṣaṇanayena.

anāhataṃ ḍamaruśabdaṃ … naditaḥ san: the participle is taken actively with an accusative object, "having sounded the unstruck sound". the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) (… stong pa nyid seng ge'i sgra sgrogs par gyur pas nag po spyod pa pa ni thod pa can no) makes the link causal and rearranges it: "because he proclaims the lion's roar of emptiness with the unstruck melody, the hero's tone, Kṛṣṇācārya is a kāpālika".

the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has nor bu'i rtsa bar rnam par gzung bar bya'o, "is to be held firm at the root of the jewel", a prescription where the Sanskrit has the absolutive vidhṛtya, "having held". For viharati bhramati it has spyod lam gyis 'chag par byed, "walks about in his deportment".

Munidatta (cp.11.m2) writes dehanagarikāṃ praviśya pracāreṇa, "having entered the town of the body, by conduct": he attaches the song's paiṭha, "entered", to the town of line 2b and takes acāre as "by conduct". The current draft of 2a reads "has entered into conduct". The Tibetan (lus kyi grong khyer du rab tu zhugs nas rab tu spyod pa) construes it as Munidatta does.

segments.translit: dvitīyapadena yogikālaṅkāram āha— āli ityādi| prathamas tāvat yogīndreṇa vajrajāpapariśodhitacandrasūryādikena ghaṇṭānūpurādiyogikālaṅkāraṃ kṛtam iti|
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he speaks of the [yogi]{yogi}'s [ornaments]{alankara}. "[Āli]{ali}" and so on. First of all, the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} has made the yogi's ornaments, [bell]{bell}, [anklet]{anklet} and the rest, with the [moon]{moon}, the [sun]{surya} and the rest, purified by [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}.
segments.note: Munidatta calls this couplet, his "second verse", the yogi's ornaments: the lord of yogis first makes bell, anklet and the rest with the moon, the sun and the rest, purified by vajra recitation (cp.11.m3). He does not say how āli and kāli, or the earrings, fit this reading.

flags.note: prathamas tāvat: nominative prathamaḥ where the adverb prathamaṃ, "first of all", is expected. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads it adverbially (dang por re zhig).

vajrajāpapariśodhitacandrasūryādikena could describe the lord of yogis ("by the lord of yogis, whose moon, sun and the rest are purified by vajra recitation") or be the means ("with the moon, the sun and the rest, purified…"). I follow the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), which takes it as the means (… zla ba dang nyi ma la sogs pas dril bu dang rkang gdub la sogs pa rnal 'byor pa'i rgyan du byed pa).
The gloss names the moon and sun of line 3b and the bell and anklet of 3a, but not āli, kāli or the earrings; whether "and the rest" is meant to cover them is not said.

segments.translit: tṛtīyapadena punar apy alaṅkāram āha— rāga ityādi| tenaiva mahāsukharāgavahninā rāgadveṣādikaṃ dagdhvā tena bhasmanā viliptāṅgo bhūya vajrasattvarūpeṇā[na]nam ālakṣya paramamokṣamuktāhāramaṇḍito hi bhramatīti|
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks again of [ornament]{alankara}. "[Passion]{raga-passion}" and so on. With that very fire of the passion of [great bliss]{mahasukha} he burns passion, [hatred]{dvesa} and the rest, and his limbs are smeared with that [ash]{ash}; then, having beheld his face in the form of [Vajrasattva]{p-vajrasattva}, adorned with the [pearl necklace]{pearl-necklace} of supreme [liberation]{moksa}, he roams.
segments.note: Munidatta reads this "third verse" as more ornament: with the fire of the passion of great bliss the yogi burns passion, hatred and the rest, smears his limbs with that ash, beholds his face in Vajrasattva's form, and roams adorned with the pearl necklace of supreme liberation (cp.11.m4). The Tibetan has "himself" (bdag) where Shastri restores "face".

flags.note: vajrasattvarūpeṇā[na]nam ālakṣya: Shastri restores [na], giving ānanam, "face". the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rdo rje sems dpa'i rang bzhin gyis bdag la dmigs te, "focusing on himself in the nature of Vajrasattva", which points to ātmānam, "himself" (restoring [tmā] instead). I translate Shastri's text; the Tibetan's reading gives the more usual sense of the yogi seeing himself as the deity.
viliptāṅgo bhūya: bhūya is taken as bhūyaḥ, "again, then", with the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) (slar yang). It could also be a loose absolutive, "having become one whose limbs are smeared".

tenaiva mahāsukharāgavahninā, "with that very fire of the passion of great bliss": the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de rnams de bzhin du bde ba chen po'i 'dod chags kyi mes, "they likewise, with the fire of the passion of great bliss", as if reading tathaiva for tenaiva.
the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) introduces the couplet as rnal 'byor pa'i rgyan, "the yogi's ornament", without punar api, "again".

segments.translit:
caturthapadena kapālacaryām āha— mārītyādi| śvāsaṃ pūrvoktamanaḥpavanaṃ tam adhikṛtya cakṣurindriyādivijñānavātaṃ nānāprakāraṃ boddhavyam| taṃ nisvabhāvīkṛtya avidyāṃ ca māyārūpāṃ prajñopāyābhedopacāreṇa kṛṣṇācāryaḥ| jagati jagadarthāśayena vajrakāpāliko bhūtvā bhramatīti|
tathā ca daṛatīpādāḥ—
prāṇī vajradharaḥ kapālavanitātulyo jagatstrījanaḥ
so 'haṃ herukamūrtir eṣa bhagavān yo naḥ prabhinno 'pi [ca]|
śrīpadmaṃ madanañ ca ṇokudahanaṃ (?) kurvan yathā gauravāt
etat sarvam atīndriyaikamanasā yogīśvaraḥ sidhyati|| 11||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks of [kāpālika]{kapalika} [conduct]{carya}. "Having killed" and so on. "The breath": the mind-[wind]{vayu} spoken of before. Under that heading, the wind of the [consciousnesses]{vijnana} of the eye faculty and the rest, of many kinds, is to be understood. Having made that [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}, and [ignorance]{avidya} too, which has the form of [illusion]{maya}, by the practice of the nondifference of [wisdom and means]{prajnopaya}, [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} becomes a [vajra]{vajra}-[kāpālika]{kapalika} in the world, intent on the welfare of the world, and roams. And so [Daṛatīpāda]{p-darati} says: "The living being is [Vajradhara]{p-vajradhara}; the womenfolk of the world are like the kāpālika's consort. I am he, this [Blessed One]{p-bhagavat} in the form of [Heruka]{p-heruka}, who is also distinct from us. Employing the glorious [lotus]{lotus}, the intoxicant and the ṇokudahana as is fitting, with reverence, the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}, with a single mind beyond the senses, is accomplished in all this."
segments.note: Munidatta reads the mother-in-law (śāsu) as breath (śvāsa), the mind-wind, with the many winds of the sense consciousnesses. Kāṇha makes these without intrinsic nature, and ignorance too, "which has the form of illusion", where the song has the mother; he then roams as a vajra-kāpālika (cp.11.m5). The Tibetan lacks "breath" and has "in the manner of an illusion".

equations.en: breath: the mind-wind spoken of before

citations.quoted: prāṇī vajradharaḥ kapālavanitātulyo jagatstrījanaḥ … etat sarvam atīndriyaikamanasā yogīśvaraḥ sidhyati ("The living being is Vajradhara; the womenfolk of the world are like the kāpālika's consort … the lord of yogis, with a single mind beyond the senses, is accomplished in all this.")
citations.work: a verse of Daṛatīpāda, as Munidatta names him (the work is not named; the Tibetan names the author da u Da'i zhabs)

flags.note: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has gsod pa zhes bya ba la sogs pa ni sngon du gsungs pa'i rlung ste / de la yid dang rlung dbang du byas te …, "'Killing' and so on: the wind spoken of before; with regard to it, taking mind and wind as the topic …". It lacks śvāsa, "breath", the word that in the Sanskrit answers the song's śāsu, so the Tibetan does not carry the reading of the mother-in-law as breath (its song line has sgyug mo, "mother-in-law").

avidyāṃ ca māyārūpāṃ: in the Sanskrit, "which has the form of illusion" describes ignorance (and stands where the song has māa, "mother"). the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de la ma rig pa yang rang bzhin med par byas la sgyu ma'i tshul gyis thabs dang shes rab dbyer med pa la nye bar spyod pa, attaching "in the manner of an illusion" to the practice of the nondifference of means and wisdom. upacāra is taken as "practice", with the Tibetan nye bar spyod pa; it can also mean "figurative usage".
pūrvokta, "spoken of before": no mind-wind is mentioned earlier in this song's comment; the reference is presumably to an earlier song.

ṇokudahanaṃ (?): Shastri himself queries the word. the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) transcribes it go ku da ha nar (…byas). I think gokudahana is the right reading: to my knowledge these syllables (go, ku, da, ha, na) are the Hevajra tradition's code for the five meats, and madana its code for liquor. That identification is mine, not Munidatta's (cp.11.m5). The translation keeps the printed "ṇokudahana" and renders madana literally as "the intoxicant".

yo naḥ prabhinno 'pi [ca]: obscure. I translate "who is also distinct from us" ([ca] is Shastri's restoration, which completes the metre). the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bcom ldan gang zhig bdag ni dbye ba med, "the Blessed One who is not different from me", which suggests reading yo no 'prabhinno 'pi, "who is not divided from us"; that scans equally in the śārdūlavikrīḍita metre.

so 'haṃ, "I am he": the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has nga rgyal dang bcas, "with pride", rendering it by sense as the pride of identifying with the deity, or reading something like sāhaṃkāra. Its he ru ka gzugs des makes "Heruka's form" instrumental.
śrīpadmaṃ madanañ ca, "the glorious lotus and the intoxicant": the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has dpal gyi pad+ma'i myos byed, "the intoxicant of the glorious lotus", joining the two words.

etat sarvam atīndriyaikamanasā yogīśvaraḥ sidhyati: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'di yis thams cad blo gros dbang po rnams / rtse gcig yid kyi rnal 'byor dbang phyug 'grub, "by this, all the lords of intellect, one-pointed in mind, become accomplished lords of yogis". It seems to divide sarva-matīndriya-, "all those of keen intellect", where I read sarvam atīndriya-, "all this … beyond the senses".
kapālavanitā is literally "skull-woman". I render it "the kāpālika's consort", with the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) (thod pa can gyi chung ma, "the skull-bearer's wife").
the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) names the author da u Da'i zhabs for Daṛatīpāda.

questions: Name forms in the commentary: Munidatta writes kṛṣṇācārya and avadhūtikā, and I have kept those spellings, linked to the entries p-kanha and avadhuti, whose English forms are "Kāṇha" and "avadhūtī" (cp.11.m1, cp.11.m2, cp.11.m5). Should the commentary keep his Sanskrit forms, which would mean adding them as listed variants, or should they be changed to the glossary's English forms? Similarly, I have given khaṭṭāṅga as "khaṭvāṅga" to match the draft.

cp.11.m4: Shastri restores vajrasattvarūpeṇā[na]nam, "his face in the form of Vajrasattva". The Tibetan bdag la dmigs, "focusing on himself", points to ātmānam, "himself". I translated Shastri's text. Do you prefer the Tibetan-supported restoration? If so, the note's last sentence changes.

cp.11.m5: Shastri queries ṇokudahanaṃ, and the Tibetan transcribes go ku da ha na. I believe gokudahana is the Hevajra code for the five meats (and madana the code for liquor), but that identification is mine, not Munidatta's. Should the translation print gokudahana, and should the woven note explain the code or keep silent?

cp.11.m5, the verse of Daṛatīpāda: yo naḥ prabhinno 'pi [ca] is obscure. The Tibetan "not different from me" suggests emending to yo no 'prabhinno 'pi, which scans equally. Should I adopt that emendation, or keep the printed "who is also distinct from us"?

cp.11.m2 and line 2a: Munidatta (dehanagarikāṃ praviśya pracāreṇa) has Kāṇha enter the town of the body and wander "by conduct", whereas the current draft of 2a reads "has entered into conduct". The draft is not mine to change, but should the line note on 2a record Munidatta's construal?

Glossary: the sasu entry cites cp.11.m5 for the reading of the mother-in-law as breath (śvāsa), but the Tibetan of that segment has no word for breath. The mother entry suggests Munidatta heard māa as māyā, but the Tibetan attaches "in the manner of an illusion" to the practice, not to ignorance (cp.11.m5). Should both entries mention this?
